paper_title: QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality-Diversity

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. In high-stakes decisions, e.g., which company to acquire or which customer to target, comparing diverse, well-reasoned options can be more useful than a single ranked list. We formalize open-ended recommendation as building a diverse, high-quality set of recommendations, each an item together with a hypothesis, a natural-language reason why the item fits the needs of a decision maker. We propose QD-Rec, a quality--diversity method that selects items with a contextual bandit and generates hypotheses with a foundation model from earlier ones kept in an archive as stepping stones. A new recommendation enters the archive if it is novel or better than its nearest neighbor. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds the largest archive in most settings.

sections.content: 20 October 2026 QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via QualityDiversity Takashi Ishida1 Taro Makino1 1Sakana AI Issa Sugiura1 Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds the largest archive in most settings. Code: github.com/SakanaAI/QD-Rec 1. Introduction Open-ended search continually produces novel and increasingly capable or diverse discoveries, and each can serve as stepping stone for further discovery (Hughes et al., 2024; Stanley and Lehman, 2015). Foundation models can act as the generator in this search, drawing on earlier candidates to write new ones. This approach has found candidates that no single query to the model would produce, including creative text (Bradley et al., 2024), adversarial prompts for red teaming (Samvelyan et al., 2024), tasks that reveal models capabilities (Lu et al., 2025), loss functions (Lu et al., 2024), faster algorithms (Novikov et al., 2025), new mathematical constructions (Novikov et al., 2025; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), agent designs (Hu et al., 2025), and self-improving agents (Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a,b). We ask whether open-ended search can extend to recommendation for decision-making. Unlike open-ended generation, where the model generates new candidates, many decisions are choices from fixed pool of candidates: an acquirer chooses among the companies that exist, reader among the papers already written, marketer among the customers. At first glance, this leaves no room for open-endedness, since the pool is finite and known in advance. However, only the items are fixed. The same item can be chosen for many different reasons, so the search over reasons is still open-ended. We therefore treat recommendation for such decisions as an open-ended search over itemhypothesis pairs. hypothesis is natural-language explanation of why an item fits the decision makers profile, such as the profile of one acquirer or one reader. The search returns diverse, high-quality set of such pairs for single profile, rather than one ranked list of items. We call this problem open-ended recommendation. In high-stakes decisions, people need to compare candidate items together with the reasons for choosing them (Aggarwal, 2016). We evaluate the set by its quality and diversity, following the qualitydiversity (QD) view of illuminating space of alternatives (Mouret and Clune, 2015). QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via QualityDiversity Figure 1 Overview of QD-Rec. Each iteration selects an item from the fixed pool via diversity-aware bandit, generates hypothesis with an LLM conditioned on archive exemplars, which act as parents (an evolutionary operator), and judges the new pair against its 𝑘 nearest neighbors: novel pair is added immediately; non-novel one survives only by winning pairwise duel against its neighbor. Open-ended recommendation has two properties that make open-ended search good fit. First, evaluation is costly: we learn recommendations value only by writing its hypothesis and judging it, so we cannot simply score every possible recommendation in advance and sort them. The system must therefore decide which item to evaluate next and learn from each result. Second, the space is larger than the pool: each item allows unlimited hypotheses, so even evaluating every item once would leave most of the space unexplored. Good hypotheses often come from adapting or combining earlier ones, so keeping modest intermediate hypotheses as stepping stones can help (Lehman and Stanley, 2011; Stanley and Lehman, 2015). QD and novelty search are well suited to such problems (Risi et al., 2025). Gallotta et al. (2024) explored QD for generating and recommending spaceship designs through grammar-based evolution guided by user preferences. We extend this connection between QD and recommendation to decisions involving fixed pool of existing items, using foundation models to generate and refine hypotheses for recommending them. We introduce QD-Rec, qualitydiversity search method for open-ended recommendation (Figure 1). In QD-Rec, an LLM called the proposer writes hypotheses, and an LLM judge or humans score them. Each iteration has three steps. contextual bandit selects an item from the candidate pool, balancing items that look promising against regions the archive has not yet covered. The proposer generates hypothesis for that item, building on few earlier hypotheses from the archive. The new recommendation is kept if it is novel, or if it is better than its nearest neighbor in the archive. Novelty and quality are thus judged locally, by comparison with nearby recommendations. Our contributions are: (i) we formalize open-ended recommendation as qualitydiversity search over itemhypothesis pairs, where the items come from fixed pool; (ii) we propose QD-Rec, with two ablations isolating its components  (Table 1)  ; and (iii) across four domains and two proposers, QD-Rec 1Evolutionary methods have been applied to decision-making more broadly, for example to evolve neural networks that prescribe interventions against COVID-19 (Risi et al., 2025, Section 6.4). 2 QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via QualityDiversity gives the highest mean quality in most LLM-judged settings, usually builds the largest archive, and outperforms diversity-aware rerankers on human-rated quality. 2. Background and Related Work We briefly review qualitydiversity methods and novelty search, evolutionary loops built around foundation models, and recommender systems. Qualitydiversity and novelty search. Qualitydiversity (QD) methods aim to discover set of high-performing yet diverse solutions rather than single optimum. Multi-dimensional Archive of Phenotypic (MAP) Elites illuminates search space by maintaining an archive and retaining elites across behavioral niches (Mouret and Clune, 2015). Novelty search emphasizes exploration by rewarding behavioral novelty, providing mechanism for stepping-stone trajectories in which intermediate solutions enable later progress (Lehman and Stanley, 2011). Recent work continues to revisit local competition and novelty definitions in QD, including dominated novelty variants (Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2025), and to reduce dependence on hand-designed behavioral descriptors through methods such as AURORA (Grillotti and Cully, 2022) and dimensionless MAP-Elites (Dharna et al., 2025). Foundation models in evolutionary loops. growing family of systems places frozen large model inside an evolutionary or QD loop as proposal operator or mutator, keeping an archive of artifacts that the model conditions on to propose the next: diverse creative text in QDAIF (Bradley et al., 2024), adversarial prompts in Rainbow Teaming (Samvelyan et al., 2024), code and program search in ELM (Lehman et al., 2023) and FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), algorithm discovery in AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), sample-efficient program evolution in ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026), open-ended evaluation tasks in Automated Capability Discovery (Lu et al., 2025), and agent designs in ADAS (Hu et al., 2025).2 separate line of work is self-referential: STOP (Zelikman et al., 2024), the Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al., 2026a), the HuxleyGödel Machine (Wang et al., 2026), and Hyperagents (Zhang et al., 2026b) turn the search on the machinery itself, so the improved scaffold or agent performs the next round of improvement. QD-Rec belongs to the first group, with itemhypothesis pairs as the artifacts. However, these systems create new artifacts, while QD-Rec must choose its items from fixed pool. Recommender systems. Recommenders learn either offline, from fixed dataset of past interactions (Aggarwal, 2016), or online, as sequential decision problem with an explorationexploitation tradeoff, usually modeled as (contextual) bandit (Agarwal et al., 2009; Agrawal and Goyal, 2013; Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020; Li et al., 2010; Song et al., 2022). Previous work has also combined bandits with QD to select parents or bins from an archive (Gallotta et al., 2024; Sfikas et al., 2021) and to choose how to generate new solutions (Cully, 2021; Gaier et al., 2020). Whereas these methods generate the candidate solutions themselves, QD-Rec uses contextual bandit to select existing items rather than parents or generation strategies. QD-Rec then generates hypotheses for the selected items. As in QD, it is evaluated by its final archive. Orthogonally, long line of work treats diversity, novelty, coverage, and serendipity as first-class objectives (Kaminskas and Bridge, 2016; McNee et al., 2006; Vargas and Castells, 2011; Ziegler et al., 2005), pursued offline by re-ranking (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998; Chen et al., 2018) and online by diversity-aware bandits (Liu et al., 2020; Radlinski et al., 2008). These methods diversify the list 2In evolutionary loops, foundation models can also play roles other than proposing new artifacts. In CycleQD (Kuroki et al., 2025) and AC/DC (Dai et al., 2026), they are themselves the artifacts being evolved. In replication of Picbreeder (Earle et al., 2026), visionlanguage models take the place of its human evaluators. 3 QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via QualityDiversity shown to user; QD-Rec instead enforces diversity at archive admission, following recent QD systems (Dharna et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025): an LLM judges whether each new pair is novel relative to its nearest archive neighbors. Finally, explainable recommendation adds natural-language explanation to each recommended item (Zhang and Chen, 2020), and so do LLM recommenders that reason before choosing or justify afterward. QD-Rec also pairs each item with reason, but it does so inside an evolutionary loop. 3. Open-Ended Recommendation Let = {𝑐1, . . . , 𝑐𝑁 } be fixed candidate pool (e.g., companies for M&A, customer profiles for targeting, papers, or books), and let 𝜋 be the profile of one decision maker. hypothesis ℎ is natural-language explanation of why an item fits 𝜋, and the hypothesis space is unbounded. recommendation is pair (𝑐, ℎ) , so the same item can be recommended several times with different hypotheses. Its quality 𝑞(𝑐, ℎ) is score from human or an LLM judge, for example on 0 to 10 scale. The score is known only after the hypothesis is written and evaluated, and each evaluation is costly. Given 𝜋 and C, the task is to return set of recommendations that have high quality and differ from one another, using at most 𝑇 evaluations. Section 5.1 defines the metrics for quality and diversity. 4. QD-Rec We present QD-Rec, an archive-based qualitydiversity (QD) method for open-ended recommendation. QD-Rec keeps an archive of retained recommendations and returns it as at the end of the run. Each new entry is compared only with its nearest neighbors in the archive to decide whether it is kept. Each archive entry 𝑥 stores recommendation (𝑐, ℎ), its embedding 𝑒 = Embed(𝑐, ℎ), and its quality score 𝑞(𝑥). The embedding is computed from structured item profile followed by the hypothesis text. The archive update then proceeds in the following two steps: Novelty check: an LLM judge is prompted with the profile 𝜋, the new entry, and its 𝑘 nearest neighbors, and returns binary decision is_novel {0, 1} (with brief reasoning). novel entry is admitted immediately; no comparison is made. Local quality comparison (only when not novel): we use blind pairwise duel: of the 𝑘 neighbors only the single nearest one is contested. It and 𝑥new are shuffled into two anonymous positions, pointwise scores are withheld, and the judge, never told which of the two is the newcomer, chooses the stronger under 𝜋 (ties are not allowed). If 𝑥new wins it replaces that neighbor; otherwise it is discarded. Algorithm 1 writes this comparison as Better𝜋. Separating the two questions keeps the retention comparison blind (the judge cannot favor or disfavor an entry for being new) and skips the comparison call entirely whenever the entry is novel. This embedding-neighborhood admission scheme is inspired by recent novelty-search/QD systems that use learned representations for similarity and archive admission (Dharna et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025). 4 QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via QualityDiversity The quality score 𝑞(𝑥) of each evaluated pair (Section 3) has two uses. The bandit reward 𝑟(𝑥) is the score divided by the maximum of its scale, so that rewards lie in [0, 1]. Reported Quality averages the score over the final archive, on its original scale. 4.2. We also define two simpler variants of QD-Rec, which serve as ablations of the full method. Novelty+Evo replaces the bandit with uniform-random item selection. Novelty removes both the bandit and the exemplars, so the proposer generates hypotheses zero-shot. All three methods share the archive update of Section 4.1, and Table 1 compares them. Algorithm 1 gives QD-Rec in full. 4.3. Implementation details To speed up experiments, we run the loop in parallel batches where workers propose and evaluate candidates against snapshot of the current archive. To select batch of 𝐵 items, we extend the single-draw rule of Section 4.2: we take 𝐵 independent posterior draws 𝜃1, . . . , 𝜃𝐵, and for each 𝜃𝑖 select the candidate maximizing 𝑠(𝑐) while excluding items already chosen in the batch and adding them to R, so the diversity bonus discourages near-duplicates within batch as well as against the archive. After each batch, we reconcile results by filtering near-duplicate additions (above cosine-similarity threshold) and resolving replacement collisions (multiple workers targeting the same neighbor). The bandit uses prior precision 𝜆 = 1 and noise standard deviation 𝜎 = 0.1, the novelty check uses 𝑘 = 3 nearest neighbors, and each run starts from 10 seed entries. 5. Experiments We evaluate the three variants (Novelty, Novelty+Evo, QD-Rec; Table 1) across four domains. 5.1. Setup Common protocol. Our main experiment uses claude-sonnet-5 as the hypothesis proposer; we additionally report weaker-proposer ablation that swaps in claude-haiku-4-5. The judge is gpt-5.6-terra in every configuration and domain, different model family from both proposers, to prevent self-preference bias (Wataoka et al., 2024). Proposer and judge both run with reasoning effort set to high. The weak-proposer ablation model does not support the effort parameter and runs without it or extended thinking. We leave the temperature setting to the provider default for claude-haiku-4-5. Novelty+Evo and QD-Rec condition each proposal on 𝑚 = 3 archive exemplars. Runs are repeated for five random seeds. Each run begins from seed archive under the same profile 𝜋; the seed controls the pipelines own sampling randomness (parent selection, item ordering) while LLM sampling stays at the provider default, so across-seed spread measures the stochasticity of the full pipeline. We embed archive entries and candidate items with OpenAIs text-embedding-3-small at 512 output dimensions, L2-normalized, and use cosine similarity for 𝑘-nearest-neighbor retrieval. Methods. We evaluate the proposed method QD-Rec and its two ablations (Novelty, Novelty+Evo) under matched evaluation budgets and shared hyperparameters within each domain. Table 1 summarizes the three variants as an ingredients view: all share the archive mechanics; Novelty+Evo adds the evolutionary few-shot operator, and QD-Rec additionally adds diversity-aware bandit item selection. Domains. We instantiate the framework on four fixed-pool domains, each realizing the hypothesis ℎ in its native genre. The first, Goodreads, is grounding check whose quality signal is real human rating rather than an LLM judge; the other three are heterogeneous applied settings. Full dataset construction (sources, filtering, pool sizes, and the specific profiles used) is in Appendix C. Goodreads. The pool is the childrens books reader has rated (Wan and McAuley, 2018); the profile 𝜋 is that reader (summarized from past reviews); ℎ is reading memo on whether they would enjoy book. Uniquely, quality is not an LLM judge but the readers own 15 rating, held out of all prompts and used only as the reward and replacement signal (Appendix C), testing whether QD still yields meaningful qualitydiversity tradeoffs under real human signal. This Quality measure evaluates the book for the reader, not the generated memo: changing the memo cannot change the rating, although it can affect novelty and archive geometry. M&A target discovery. is universe of 6,332 US companies built from LSEG Workspace data (business descriptions, industry taxonomy, financials). The business descriptions average approximately 123 words. The profile 𝜋 is an acquirer (Walt Disney or JPMorgan Chase), and ℎ is an acquisition thesis (e.g. capability acquisition vs. market access vs. vertical integration). Deal sourcing motivates it: teams want diverse set of strategic theses rather than single shortlist. Marketing. is 10,000 synthetic customer profiles from California, sampled from NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-USA (Meyer and Corneil, 2025). The customer profiles average approximately 685 words. The profile 𝜋 is product (a desktop 3D printer or an online upskilling subscription), and ℎ is targeting hypothesis explaining why profile is an attractive target for 𝜋, yielding map of distinct targeting angles rather than ranked list. Candidate embeddings for bandit item selection are precomputed from title+abstract; archive embeddings are computed from title+abstract+memo. Evaluation. Four metrics summarize runs final active archive. Quality is the mean pointwise score of its entries: the judge score (010), or in Goodreads the readers real star rating (15). Diversity is one minus the mean pairwise cosine similarity between archive-entry embeddings, computed in the original embedding space (the complement of the mean pairwise similarity used to quantify homogenization by Jiang et al., 2025). Conclusion We introduced QD-Rec, an archive-based qualitydiversity method for open-ended recommendation, where the items are chosen with contextual bandits, and the reasons for recommending them are searched open-endedly. Across four domains, QD-Rec gave the best mean Quality in most settings and usually built the largest archive. As first work along this line, we kept it relatively simple, and several directions follow. 10 QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via QualityDiversity First, our bandit uses Bayesian linear regression to model reward from fixed item embeddings. Neural contextual bandits (Zhang et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2020) could capture nonlinear relationships between these embeddings and reward. More radically, the bandit could be discarded altogether in favor of coding agent that reads the archive directly, reasons over which regions look exhausted and which look promising, and writes its own selection rule, replacing fixed parametric reward model with policy that can be inspected and revised in natural language. Second, exemplars are sampled uniformly from the archive, and could instead be selected by quality, recency, or how often they have already served as exemplars (Earle et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Bandits could also be used for parent selection, in addition to item selection (Gallotta et al., 2024; Sfikas et al., 2021). Third, this work focused on the outer loop: which item to evaluate next, and which pairs to retain. The inner hypothesis generator was single prompted LLM call, and could instead be full research agent (Lin et al., 2026; Shang et al., 2025); we kept it lightweight to show that the outer loop is itself meaningful lever, and expect the two to compose.
